local_facts.claim: North Carolina General Statute § 97-10.1 provides that when an employee and employer are subject to and comply with the Workers’ Compensation Act, the rights and remedies granted by the Act exclude other rights and remedies against the employer for the injury or death.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A covered Concord work injury may proceed through workers’ compensation instead of an ordinary personal-injury lawsuit against the employer. The first legal task is identifying the work relationship and whether a separate party, such as a contractor, property owner, or equipment maker, may be involved.
local_facts.title: A job injury may have a different legal route

local_facts.claim: The North Carolina Industrial Commission’s Form 18 instructions say the form establishes a legal claim when filed within the stated period and that an employer’s Form 19 does not satisfy the employee’s obligation to file a claim.
local_facts.why_it_matters: After a Concord work injury, an employer incident report is not the same thing as the employee’s claim. Keeping copies, reporting promptly, and identifying the Industrial Commission process early can prevent the file from being treated as complete when it is not.
local_facts.title: An employer report is not the employee’s claim

local_facts.claim: The City of Concord reports that Concord-Padgett Regional Airport supports 4,430 local jobs, has 226 based aircraft, and is home to NASCAR’s air force and several flight schools.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A serious incident in Concord can arise in an airport, motorsports, manufacturing, or contractor setting with more than one company at the site. Sorting the employer, staffing company, contractor, property operator, and equipment roles directs the search for the right records and claim path.
local_facts.title: Concord work sites can involve several separate roles

anchors.label: Statutory percentage for an injury contingency
anchors.detail: The State Bar rule bars a clearly excessive fee and gives eight factors for testing one. No North Carolina statute or rule assigns a percentage to a negligence recovery.

anchors.label: General Court of Justice fee, superior court civil action
anchors.detail: Paid to the Clerk of Superior Court in Concord when the complaint is filed, alongside a $16 facilities fee and a $4.00 telecommunications and data connectivity charge.

anchors.label: Fee a judge can tax against an insurer that refused to negotiate
anchors.detail: Available where damages recovered are $25,000 or less and the recovery beat the highest offer made ninety days before trial. It adds money for the injured side.

anchors.label: Ceiling on a medical provider's lien, not on a lawyer's fee
anchors.detail: Measured exclusive of attorneys' fees, and the statute says nothing in it interferes with amounts due for attorney's services. It limits what doctors and hospitals claim.

fee_rows.stage: The contingency percentage in a Concord injury claim
fee_rows.share: Set by agreement, tested for excess
fee_rows.note: The eight factors include the customary charge in this locality, the amount involved and the result, the skill required, and whether the arrangement was fixed or contingent.

fee_rows.share: Client-signed writing, plus a closing statement
fee_rows.note: The agreement states the percentages on settlement, trial and appeal, which expenses are deducted, and when. At the end the lawyer furnishes a written statement of outcome and remittance.

fee_rows.stage: Filing a notice of hearing on a motion
fee_rows.note: Charged for motions not already priced in the clerk's separate schedule, and assessed once for each motion rather than once for the case.

fee_rows.stage: Recovering the cost of a private process server
fee_rows.share: Actual cost or $50, whichever is less
fee_rows.note: The lower figure controls unless the court makes a finding that serving that defendant was difficult. Expert witness charges are assessable only for time actually spent testifying.

fee_rows.stage: A Medicaid claim reaching into the settlement
fee_rows.note: That presumption applies where the agency's claim exceeds a third, and the injured person may dispute it by application within thirty days under a clear and convincing standard.

fee_rows.stage: Malpractice noneconomic damages, a different case type
fee_rows.note: Applies to claims against health care providers, resets every third year by consumer price index, and disappears entirely where disfigurement or death meets reckless conduct.
